title: The archbishop, also called Hawk and Warlord

steps.title: See it
steps.text: The archbishop moves as a bishop or as a knight: along a diagonal as far as it likes, or with a knight's jump. It takes the same way. It comes from Capablanca chess, played on a board ten squares wide, where each side has one and a pawn may promote to it. Seirawan chess has the same piece under the name hawk, and there players bring it into the game from hand, onto the square a back-rank piece has just left. In Spartan chess it is one of the Spartans' pieces, the warlord. The marked squares are every square it can reach.

steps.title: Try it
steps.text: Move the archbishop to the marked square, one square straight ahead. It can't step straight, so combine a bishop move and a knight jump: it takes two moves.

pages.text: The archbishop is worth nearly as much as a queen, and more than a rook. A bishop stays on squares of one colour, but the archbishop's knight jump always lands on the other colour, so it can reach every square. Here it can run along the diagonal to h8, or jump to e6, a square of the other colour.

Its knight jump gives forks. (A fork is a move that attacks two pieces at once.) Here the archbishop goes along the diagonal to e7, and from there its knight move attacks both the king on g8 and the rook on c8. The king must get out of check, and then the archbishop takes the rook.

It can't move straight, so a rook can attack it along a file or a rank and it can't hit back. Here the black rook on d6 attacks it from two squares away. The archbishop must step off the rook's lines, here to f2.

puzzles.prompt: Win the black archbishop in two moves.
puzzles.hint: The black king and its archbishop stand on one diagonal. Check the king along it, so that it has to step aside.
Your king covers a2 and b2. Check along a diagonal from a square whose knight jump also covers b1.
